newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Saudi job goals remain far removed from reality.
newsitem.headline: Saudi job goals remain far removed from reality.

text.p: "Announcement of recruitment for Saudis only", reads a job advertisement in a Saudi daily. It is one of a new brand of ads mushrooming in the country's press.
A few years ago such advertisements were rare, as employers in the oil-rich kingdom looked for cheap foreign workers to fill job vacancies from garbage collector to medical specialist.

Today Saudi newspapers are replete with advertisements for qualified nationals as the government -- faced with a burgeoning population and a state spending squeeze -- struggles to replace the country's huge expatriate workforce with home-grown workers.

"Saudisation" -- the policy to substitute some of the 12 million Saudis for the six million expatriate workers -- has become a top government goal in the world's biggest oil producer and exporter. Whether it will be a success remains to be seen.
The topic is on everyone's tongue, from King Fahd to foreign workers fretting for their jobs.
"Whenever the king speaks, he never forgets to mention Saudisation," said Sharif Mohammad, senior economic adviser at The Economic Bureau, a private Saudi think-tank.
SAUDISATION STILL FALLS SHORT OF HOPES
But despite the royal directives and official targets, analysts say Saudisation has fallen short of expectations.
Nationals still make up less than seven percent of private sector employees and unemployment among Saudis could be as high as 20 percent, they say. There are no official jobless figures.

"Saudisation is not working like the Saudis had imagined," one analyst said. "They thought it could be done with appeals to businesses, but that didn't work. Then they tried pressure and penalties, but even now it's not working as well as they hoped."

To push the Saudisation drive, the government has ordered all private firms employing more than 20 people to increase their Saudi manpower by five percent annually. It has also said it will completely phase foreigners out of some jobs -- from limousine drivers to shipping workers.
Foreign workers are mostly from the Indian subcontinent, Egypt, other Arab countries and southeast Asia.
SAUDIS ARE MORE EXPENSIVE THAN EXPATRIATES
"The Saudi government is aggressively pursuing the policy of Saudisation," a Riyadh-based diplomat said.

"But for all companies it is a cost factor because Saudis are more expensive. The Saudi worker will cost more than the expatriate he replaces but will generally work less," he added, echoing comments made by several business executives.

With half of its citizens under the age of 15 and the population burgeoning at an estimated 3.5 to four percent a year -- one of the highest levels in the world -- Saudi Arabia faces a formidable task integrating its youth into the workforce.
"If the government fails to meet the aspirations of the young people, they may turn to alternatives such as the opposition," a diplomat said.
The country's 1995-2000 development plan set a target of creating 659,000 jobs for Saudi citizens by the turn of the millennium, in part by phasing foreigners out.

Expatriates in many white-collar positions are feeling the squeeze. But analysts say the government measures do not go far enough, as the plan foresees the size of the Saudi working-age population increasing by 1.6 million in the same period.
"The main problem...is that there is not enough time to implement a sensible idea," one said. "There are too many young people whose job requirements have to be met too quickly."
SAUDIS USED TO OFFICE JOBS

Since oil brought prosperity to the desert kingdom, Saudis have been employed predominantly in the state sector where they enjoyed half-day office jobs. But tight fiscal policy due to low oil prices in the early 1990s and huge Gulf war costs trimmed the cushion of wealth in the kingdom.
"The government has emphasised that it is saturated in terms of Saudisation," an economic expert said.
Analysts say many Saudis lacked the work ethic and skills to meet the requirements of the job market. They said education was too focused on liberal arts with too little vocational training.
Only five percent of Saudis do vocational training, and most consider a university degree far more prestigious, analysts say.

"The private sector doesn't want to hire Saudis because they come late, don't work as hard as foreigners, they are very difficult to fire because of strict labour laws and they don't have the skills that are needed," the economic expert said.
SAUDI ATTITUDES ARE CHANGING
Diplomats said Saudis still frowned upon doing manual labour, although attitudes were slowly changing.
"They'll accept 1,000 riyals ($265) a month jobs now which they would have shunned a few years ago," one said.
Saudi annual per capita income is among the Gulf's lowest at about $7,000, compared to $16,800 in neighbouring Kuwait.

"Driving a taxi is OK, being an errand runner is OK. A toilet cleaner is not," one said. "But some are agreeing to do jobs like loading and unloading at bottling factories. They usually don't last long, but they turn up for work initially."
($1=3.75 riyals)
